authors.name: Btissame El Mahtout, Florian Ziel

papers.title: RefDecoder: Enhancing Visual Generation with Conditional Video Decoding
papers.summary: Video generation powers a vast array of downstream applications. However, while the de facto standard, i.e., latent diffusion models, typically employ heavily conditioned denoising networks, their decoders often remain unconditional. We observe that this architectural asymmetry leads to significant loss of detail and inconsistency relative to the input image. To address this, we argue that the decoder requires equal conditioning to preserve structural integrity. We introduce RefDecoder, a reference-conditioned video VAE decoder by injecting high-fidelity reference image signal directly into the decoding process via reference attention. Specifically, a lightweight image encoder maps the reference frame into the detail-rich high-dimensional tokens, which are co-processed with the denoised video latent tokens at each decoder up-sampling stage. We demonstrate consistent improvements across several distinct decoder backbones (e.g., Wan 2.1 and VideoVAE+), achieving up to +2.1 dB PSNR over the unconditional baselines on the Inter4K, WebVid, and Large Motion reconstruction benchmarks. Notably, RefDecoder can be directly swapped into existing video generation systems without additional fine-tuning, and we report across-the-board improvements in subject consistency, background consistency, and overall quality scores on the VBench I2V benchmark. Beyond I2V, RefDecoder generalizes well to a wide range of visual generation tasks such as style transfer and video editing refinement.

authors.name: Xiang Fan, Yuheng Wang, Bohan Fang, Zhongzheng Ren, Ranjay Krishna

papers.title: Growing a Neural Network in Breadth, Depth, and Time
papers.summary: Brains and AI systems alike must achieve their goals with limited space, time, energy, and data. Here we focus on space and time, defining differentiable costs for breadth (channels), depth (layers), and time (recurrent steps) in a recurrent convolutional network. We optimize these costs jointly with task error via backpropagation. Pricing each resource differently, we grow a diverse set of computational graphs through optimization. We find that breadth, depth, and time can be traded off against each other at a given level of accuracy. Networks grow with task complexity and, when allowed to adaptively allocate time per input, take more recurrent steps if inputs are occluded. The time the model spends on each image also correlates with human reaction times, despite no training on human data. Our work takes a step toward a normative account of how spatial and temporal resource costs jointly shape neural architectures in brains and machines.

authors.name: Eivinas Butkus, Kedar Garz\'on Gupta, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

papers.title: Reactivity-Informed Machine Learning for Performance Prediction and Design Space Exploration of Alkali-Activated Slag
papers.summary: Establishing quantitative relationships among mix design, raw material properties, curing conditions, and performance remains a long-standing challenge in cementitious materials, particularly for alkali-activated materials with variable precursor and activator chemistry. Here, we curated the largest literature-derived alkali-activated slag (AAS) dataset to date, comprising over 3100 compressive strength records, 155 chemically distinct ground granulated blast-furnace slags (GGBSs), and 24 attributes incorporating precursor chemistry, fineness, and reactivity. Multiple machine learning (ML) algorithms were benchmarked across progressively enriched feature scenarios, demonstrating that integrating GGBS compositions, fineness, curing conditions, and specimen geometry improves predictive performance. The average metal oxide dissociation energy (AMODE), a physically interpretable representation of precursor reactivity, provides a compact alternative descriptor to explicit oxide compositions while enabling comparable predictive performance. Model interpretation revealed physically consistent trends from heterogeneous data, including non-monotonic effects of Na2O dosage and silicate modulus, reduced predicted strength at higher water content and larger specimen size, and coupled oxide-level effects more coherently represented by AMODE than by individual oxide contents. Statistically constrained design space exploration reveals reactivity-dependent trade-offs among strength, embodied CO2 emissions, and cost. The design maps identify high-strength regions with substantially lower CO2 emissions than OPC-based references at similar cost. Overall, this work demonstrates how reactivity-informed ML can extract physically meaningful trends from heterogeneous AAS data and guide source-dependent binder design. The curated dataset is publicly accessible to support advances in cement and concrete research.

authors.name: Qiyao He, Zhanzhao Li, Kai Gong

papers.title: AlphaWiSE: Adaptive Weight Interpolation for Continual Multimodal Representation Learning
papers.summary: Multimodal retrieval models align audio, images, and text in a shared embedding space, but sequential adaptation can degrade cross-modal relationships learned in earlier phases. Existing continual-learning procedures produce a single final checkpoint, so every retrieval direction shares the same stability-plasticity trade-off. We introduce AlphaWiSE, a post-hoc weight-space interpolation method that combines a sequential fine-tuning endpoint with a companion endpoint obtained with a stability-oriented continual-learning method. AlphaWiSE fits one scalar interpolation coefficient for each corresponding parameter tensor on an exemplar memory while both endpoints remain frozen. The interpolated tensors are then materialized into a single checkpoint, so the deployed model retains the architecture and inference cost of a single backbone. On continual audio-image-text retrieval, the fused model improves on the better of its two endpoints in 13 of 18 average retrieval measures and on the fixed blend of the same checkpoints in 25 of 36 measures. Its pairings achieve the strongest average audio-to-text and image-to-audio retrieval among all compared methods. Project page: https://alphawise.cvmlgroup.web.illinois.edu/

authors.name: Sarthak Jain, Qiran Hu, Zhen Zhu, Yaoyao Liu

papers.title: An Analytically Trained Variational Quantum Circuit using the Output Probability Distribution of Quantum Phase Estimation on NISQ Hardware
papers.summary: Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) is the standard algorithm for molecular ground-state energy estimation and often serves as a subroutine in larger quantum algorithms, but its deep circuits make it impractical on current noisy hardware. A previous variational approach replaces the QPE subroutine with a shallow Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) trained to reproduce the QPE measurement distribution, but generates the training target by classically simulating the full QPE circuit, which is prohibitive for molecules. We reformulate this idea, computing the training target analytically from the Dirichlet kernel, using only a reference energy, the number of ancilla qubits and the evolution time, so the controlled-unitary and inverse-QFT operations of QPE are never simulated. Using H$_2$, we select the VQC stepwise by comparing its IBM Quantum hardware output with the target using four metrics. We first choose the entangler (linear or full) and number of layers of an $R_Y$-$R_Z$-$CZ$ ansatz, with and without dynamical decoupling (DD). As DD degraded performance with depth, we then choose, without DD, the ansatz ($R_Y$-$R_Z$-$CZ$ or $R_Y$-$CZ$) and the training simulator (ideal or noisy). The configuration fixed on H$_2$, a single-layer linear-entangler $R_Y$-$CZ$ ansatz trained on the ideal simulator, is validated on LiH, H$_2$O, BeH$_2$, NH$_3$, CH$_4$, O$_2$ and N$_2$, recovering the dominant QPE bitstring on hardware with errors within chemical accuracy ($1.59 \times 10^{-3}$ Ha) for all eight molecules at the chosen evolution times. We also analyze the hardware side lobes of both ans\"atze, and a noise analysis of the selected ansatz at 8 and 64 layers examines how DD performs with depth. As training requires a known reference energy, the surrogate is not meant for standalone energy estimation, but can replace the QPE subroutine where a larger algorithm uses only its measurement outcome.

authors.name: Mousumi Kundu, Ashish Kumar Patra, Anurag K. S. V., Ruchika Bhat, Sai Shankar P., Alok Shukla, Jaiganesh G

papers.title: Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting: Robust Inference under Deterministic and Random Distribution Shifts
papers.summary: Reweighting source samples to match a target covariate distribution is a standard response to distribution shift when generalizing evidence across populations. It is well suited to deterministic, learnable covariate discrepancies, but can fail when source--target differences extend beyond covariate shift or when estimation of the density-ratio weights is unstable. We introduce a new model where the discrepancy between two population laws comprises a deterministic covariate shift and a non-systematic component, modeled as random perturbation of the probability space. This separates systematic shifts, treated as bias and corrected by reweighting, from random perturbations, treated as distributional uncertainty and reduced by dataset pooling. Under pure random perturbations, this principle yields Augmented Inverse Distance Weighting, which combines regression augmentation with variance-optimal dataset-level pooling and attains asymptotic variance no larger than exact covariate balancing. When both components are present, we develop Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting, which interpolates between AIDW and standard augmented importance weighting. Both estimators tradeoff sampling and distributional uncertainty via a distributional distance quantifying the strength of random perturbations. We establish asymptotic normality of both estimators and provide tuning and diagnostic tools. On three real-world multi-site datasets exhibiting diverse distribution shifts, the proposed methods consistently reduce mean-squared error compared with weighting baselines, and improve empirical coverage when covariate-shift adjustment alone undercovers.

authors.name: Ying Jin, Dominik Rothenh\"ausler

papers.title: SiMDex: Mining Similar Egocentric Videos for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Manipulation
papers.summary: Recent years have witnessed an explosive trend of scaling ego-centric human videos for robot manipulation, yet it remains unclear which data actually benefits dexterous manipulation. We present SiMDex, a similarity-based data mining framework that casts human data selection for VLA post-training in dexterous manipulation as a recommendation problem. For each robot demonstration, SiMDex runs a recall-ranking-re-ranking cascade over ~32M egocentric human samples: two stages, recall and ranking, select a task-relevant subset in a morphology-agnostic action space, and re-ranking verifies it on pixels, with no change to VLA architecture or training. Against a strong baseline trained with an equal amount of randomly sampled human data, SiMDex uses only ~1.49M mined samples (<5% of the pool) yet improves the overall success rate from 47.7% to 61.7%, showing that selective curation outperforms indiscriminate data mixing.

authors.name: Nie Lin, Takehiko Ohkawa, Sijin Chen, Ruoshi Wen, Zhuohang Li, Liqun Huang, Zhengming Zhu, Yiming Bao, Yunfei Li, Minjie Cai, Xiao Ma, Wei Xu, Yoichi Sato

papers.title: Fractal dimension predicts quantum kernel collapse in angle-encoded data
papers.summary: Angle-encoded quantum kernels on tabular data collapse when the feature map is wider than the intrinsic dimension of the data. We propose the correlation fractal dimension D2 as an a priori qubit budget: encode D2 coordinates chosen by FD-ASE instead of the PCA-95% width or all E attributes. On nine data sets and a statevector simulator (n= 32), a one-layer ZZ fidelity kernel at q=D2 stays geometrically alive while the same kernel at the PCA-95% width has already collapsed. The budget is map-dependent: product-state and IQP maps overshoot it; a second ZZ layer undershoots it. Packed dense-angle and re-uploading encodings still live at the fractal q, but not when PCA-95% features are stacked onto those qubits. Shrinking the angle bandwidth moves the ZZ knee later; stretching it kills the kernel earlier. On IBM Quantum (ibm_fez, 256 shots, n=8) the one-layer ZZ kernel at the fractal width matches the exact kernel (MAE 0.021); past that width both hardware and simulator have collapsed. The ceiling is a property of the map-data pair at a stated bandwidth, not of the classical table alone.

authors.name: Ana Paula Appel

papers.title: Self-Supervised Learning for Robust Resonance Mass Regression in Cascade Decays
papers.summary: Reconstructing the mass of a heavy resonance from its decay products with missing energy is one of the central tasks that directly determine the sensitivity in new physics searches at collider experiments. Supervised learning approaches to this problem often struggle to generalize well due to the presence of various systematic uncertainties and distribution shifts. Exhausting all possible variations in the labeled data can be very compute-intensive, while a failure of the model to generalize can corrupt the reconstructed resonance widths that are critical in peak-hunting analyses. In this work, following the foundation model paradigm, we use a self-supervised approach to pre-train a transformer encoder with VICReg to learn an embedding invariant to various corruptions, then fine-tune it for mass regression on a heavy resonance with masses ranging from 2.5 to 6.5 TeV and a SUSY-like cascade decay into an eleven-body final state. We show that the pre-trained model reconstructs sharper resonance peaks and has a more stable performance under various realistic corruptions, compared to a supervised model of the same architecture trained on the same augmented data from scratch.

authors.name: Ho Fung Tsoi, Alex Yang, Luis Felipe Gutierrez Zagazeta, Shion Chen, Dylan Sheldon Rankin

papers.title: Similarity Pairing with Energy Mover's Distance for Self-Supervised Pre-Training at the LHC
papers.summary: Many self-supervised methods for training foundation models at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) rely on data augmentations to encourage the model to embed events into a representation space invariant to certain physical or detector symmetries. A common challenge arises from the large freedom in choosing a proper set of augmentations on which downstream performance depends. The implementation of augmentations involves either modifying existing events, potentially breaking the event fidelity, or simulating more event variants, which is computationally intensive. In this work, we present a data-driven method of pairing events by their similarity via the energy mover's distance (EMD), which measures how similar two events are in terms of the work required to transform one into the other. With this approach, distinct events are sampled and matched by their similarity to serve as views for learning invariance, keeping the physics content of each event intact without handcrafted distortions. We demonstrate this augmentation-free pairing method by pre-training on QCD jets via self-distillation and show that it can yield semantic jet embeddings with downstream discrimination power comparable to or better than an augmentation-based baseline.

authors.name: Ho Fung Tsoi, Dylan Sheldon Rankin

papers.title: AECSF: Adaptive Ensemble Conditional Score Filtering for High-Dimensional Nonlinear Data Assimilation
papers.summary: In high-dimensional filters, particle weights can concentrate on a few members, while Gaussian updates can miss non-Gaussian posterior structure. A diffusion filter updates a forecast ensemble by gradually denoising particles in light of a new observation. Each noisy particle can correspond to several system states, and these states can have very different likelihoods. A score correction based on a single state can therefore misrepresent the posterior. We propose the Adaptive Ensemble Conditional Score Filter (AECSF), which uses the conditional Tweedie identity to express the required score through the mean state given the particle and the observation. All reverse particles share a set of proposals, but each assigns its own weights to estimate its conditional mean. As denoising proceeds, the reverse particles guide which proposals are resampled. We characterize when fixed proposals yield the exact noisy posterior score and bound the contribution of conditional-mean errors to the final sampling error. In controlled Gaussian experiments, AECSF samples the posterior more accurately than the tested likelihood-guidance rules. With 20 forecast members in 10,000-dimensional Lorenz-96, AECSF has lower RMSE and CRPS than the tested tempered SMC and kernel-density filters. On Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, the analysis ensembles also improve subsequent forecasts over the tested baselines at comparable cost. For Navier-Stokes flow, we learn a forecast prior that captures spatial dependence in vorticity and use it to reconstruct the full field from sparse velocity measurements.

authors.name: Yangwen Zhang, Shiwei Ni, Xiaoping Zhang, Xiaofei Guan, Lili Ju

papers.title: A Dynamical Theory of LoRA in Continual Learning
papers.summary: Despite the widespread use of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), little is known about its dynamics in continual learning and the mechanisms by which low-rank updates affect catastrophic forgetting. We provide an asymptotically exact dynamical characterization of LoRA in a solvable two-task teacher-student model. In the high-dimensional online-learning limit, we derive a closed system of ordinary differential equations for a finite set of macroscopic order parameters, yielding exact expressions for the generalization errors throughout both the initial Task 1 learning phase and the subsequent LoRA fine-tuning on Task 2. The theory quantitatively matches finite-dimensional simulations and exposes two characteristic effects of LoRA: when the first-task representation is not yet specialized, low-rank adaptation reduces interference with features learned on the first task, but its initialization slows adaptation to the second task. Building on this mechanistic picture, we analyze a state-dependent masking strategy that freezes hidden units carrying the strongest first-task representations and restricts adaptation to the complementary subspace. This structural partitioning markedly reduces forgetting, while preserving plasticity on the new task. Our framework further clarifies the role of adapter rank: transfer improves only up to the intrinsic dimensionality of the target task and saturates beyond it, while forgetting continues to grow with rank. These results provide a dynamical and geometric account of how low-rank adaptation organizes information across sequential tasks, and are qualitatively reproduced on sequential MNIST and CIFAR-100 using a shallow network and ResNet-18, respectively.

authors.name: Th\'eo Marchetta, Filippo Alessandroni, Alessandro Breccia, Alessandro Ingrosso, Federica Gerace

papers.title: NucleoNet: A Nuclear-Aware Determinant Ansatz for Multi-Geometry Neural Variational Monte Carlo
papers.summary: Neural-network variational Monte Carlo provides an accurate route to solving the electronic Schr\"odinger equation, but many neural wavefunctions are optimized for a single nuclear geometry, requiring separate calculations to map out a potential energy surface. We introduce NucleoNet, a nuclear-aware determinant ansatz that jointly evolves electronic and nuclear representations through a shared backbone, with antisymmetry enforced by electronic determinants. Across eight equilibrium small-molecule benchmarks, NucleoNet achieves energies comparable to established neural-wavefunction baselines with substantially fewer trainable parameters, totaling 0.10--0.13 million. For each molecular system, a single model optimized jointly across geometries describes the N$_2$ dissociation curve, Li displacement in LiCN, and the ethane and formamide minimum-energy paths for bond dissociation. Models trained on sparse geometry sets generalize to unseen configurations in N$_2$ and LiCN without further optimization. For N$_2$, training on six geometries yields a mean absolute error (MAE) of $1.13\ \mathrm{m}E_h$ on a 32-point evaluation grid, compared with $1.07\ \mathrm{m}E_h$ when optimized on all 32 geometries. Ablation studies on N$_2$ show that propagating nuclear representations improves geometric generalization under both shared and nucleus-specific envelope parameterizations.

authors.name: Qiao Gao, Yang Huang, Enze Hou, Yuzhi Liu, Jingrun Chen, Han Wang

papers.title: CoCoNet: Convex Conformal Network for Multi-Dimensional Uncertainty Regions
papers.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free coverage guarantees under exchangeability, but the efficiency of its prediction regions depends critically on the choice of the conformity score. This is particularly important in multivariate regression, where dependencies across output dimensions induce complex joint uncertainty structures. This paper introduces CoCoNet (Convex Conformal Network) for learning conformity scores that induce flexible and data-adaptive prediction regions. The main mechanism is an input-dependent convex score learned end-to-end: CoCoNet trains the score on held-out data by directly minimizing the size of its sublevel sets, while enforcing convexity with respect to the residual so that every prediction region is inherently convex. CoCoNet then applies split-conformal calibration to retain finite-sample coverage guarantees. The paper presents two variants of the method: 1) CoCoNet-Spline, based on piecewise-linear scores aggregated by an $\ell_\infty$ or an $\ell_1$ norm, which induce hyper-rectangular and polytope prediction regions, respectively; and 2) CoCoNet-ICNN, based on Input Convex Neural Networks, which induces more flexible convex regions. Experiments compare CoCoNet with other CP baselines over synthetic and real-world datasets with output dimensions ranging from 2 to 16. These results demonstrate the importance of learning input-adaptive conformity scores directly from the data.

authors.name: Alireza Moradi, Thomas Bruys, Pascal Van Hentenryck, Reza Zandehshahvar

papers.title: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
papers.summary: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together. The benchmark and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MemJoin-01BF/.

authors.name: Qishun Yang, Shu Yang, Difei Xu, Di Wang, Meng Ding

papers.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
papers.summary: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano, MemT-1.0-Flash, and MemT-1.0-Pro, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

authors.name: Zhiyu Li, Zeyu Zhang, Linyun Liu, Yiwei Bu, Chenyang Xi, Xichong Zhang, Yi Yu, Yu Yu, Zhichen Liu, Yuxiao Yi, Chunyu Li, Haoran Liu, Zhenkai Ding, Le Zhou, Juncheng Zhang, Boyu Chen, Zehao Lin, Guorui Li, Renyu Fu, Ji Li, Youyang Xia, Jiajun Shen, Harvey Li, Jinsong Zhou, Helan Hu, Tong Shen, Tianxiao Xu, Chenye Han, Weijie Li, Zhongquan Zhou, Hongming Xu, Yuekeng Li, Erenkai Zhu, Peng Yu, Wenhao Li, Jingyi Kang, Xixuan Hao, Xuzhou Zhu, Can Chen, Jiawei Liu, Chen Jiang, Tao Jiang, Fangwei Xiang, Zepeng Yao, Kai Chen, Guang Yang, Mingfei Lu, Chunhui Li, Zhengxuan Jiang, Bo Tang, Shiyu Zhan, Yihang Sun, Jie Chu, Wenjun Xiong, Zhenxiang Hua, Chen Lin, Detong Su, Dongyu Deng, Qiuping Ding, Guofeng Ding, Si Chen, Guohua Wen, Xu Chen, Zhi-Qin John Xu, Ying-Cong Chen, Ningyu Zhang, Haofen Wang, Muning Wen, Haotian Chen, Wentao Zhang, Xuanhe Zhou, Rita Zhang, Junchi Yan, Feiyu Xiong

papers.title: Two $\operatorname{ReLU}$ Layers is All You Need
papers.summary: We prove that every $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network can be exactly simulated by a $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network with two hidden layers. We present two proofs: one that is based on fillings in homological algebra and a direct combinatorial proof.

authors.name: Florestan Brunck, Christoph Hertrich, Kilian Ruess, Jack Stade, Amir Yehudayoff

papers.title: Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories
papers.summary: Quantization-aware training (QAT) aims to recover reasoning capabilities in low-bit large language models (LLMs). Existing recipes typically supervise the quantized student with the original full-precision model on fixed response sequences. However, the resulting low-bit quantized models still struggle on long-horizon reasoning tasks and often fail to terminate within a token budget that suffices for the full-precision model. We identify two challenges in closing this gap. First, fixed-response supervision leaves a mismatch between training prefixes and those encountered during student generation, and this trajectory divergence grows as responses lengthen. Second, on its own prefixes, the student underpredicts some next-token candidates and overpredicts others, and this distributional misalignment becomes more frequent at high-entropy prefixes. We present OnQ, a low-bit recovery pipeline that combines on-policy distillation and candidate-wise Dynamic KL. Starting from block-wise calibration, the quantized student generates responses and receives full-precision teacher supervision on its own prefixes. Dynamic KL weights forward and reverse KL by each candidate's teacher-student probability ratio to balance correction of under- and overprediction. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, OnQ achieves the highest nine-benchmark average, with the largest gains on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks. At 2 bits, it outperforms every baseline on every benchmark at every model size, improving the Qwen3-8B average by 10.26 points over the strongest baseline. It also produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitive errors.

authors.name: Boyuan Zheng, Jing Xiong, Chenwei Wu, Hui Shen, Zesen Zhao, Hei Ting Una Chan, Xueshen Liu, Zhen Zhang, Liyue Shen, Zechun Liu, Z. Morley Mao

papers.title: ReDence: A Hybrid Agentic and System One Model Framework for Rapid, Evidence-Grounded Detection of Social Engineering Scams
papers.summary: Detecting online social engineering (SE) scams often requires examining website workflows, verifying claims against external sources, and connecting evidence across multiple pages. Existing detectors provide limited support for these tasks and rarely produce actionable evidence to support their decisions, leaving analysts to manually investigate flagged websites, which inevitably delays detection and subsequent takedown of these attacks. To address this gap, we present ReDence, a hybrid framework for automated, evidence-grounded scam investigation, detection, and reporting across diverse SE scam categories. ReDence combines two locally deployed, fine-tuned models: a multimodal agentic Investigator (Qwen3.5-4B) for investigative planning, evidence interpretation, and report generation, and a specialized System One model (Tev1) that handles binary and multiple-choice decisions, including browser action selection and evidence assessment, significantly reducing response generation overhead while preserving the Investigator's reasoning capabilities for complex tasks. The reports produced by ReDence also document investigative actions, collected evidence, and the reasoning behind each decision. Our evaluation shows that ReDence has a detection accuracy of over 96%, outperforming existing detectors while being at least four times faster. When deployed on a real-world URL stream over the period of 28 days, ReDence identified 4,042 new SE scam websites across 17 categories, of which at least 71% were missed by all four popular anti-scam blocklists evaluated. Feedback from twelve domain providers indicated that ReDence's investigative reports helped analysts recognize the scams documented in reported websites, understand the supporting evidence, and validate cases more efficiently. We open-source ReDence to aid automated, evidence-grounded scam investigation and reporting.

authors.name: Jaishnoor Kaur, Josef Hor\'a\v{c}ek, Ian Waskom, Sayak Saha Roy

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to train robust, adaptable systems across healthcare, e-commerce, and robotics. In these settings, legal, ethical, or logistical concerns may preclude certain key variables that drive decisions from being collected during deployment time. This gives rise to a setting known as runtime confounding: the logged data hold full observability, but deployment time lacks knowledge of certain variables, known as runtime confounders. Unlike single timepoint and non-adaptive settings, runtime confounding under reinforcement learning has the potential to propagate over time, as earlier decisions affect future states, observations, and action assignments, leading to biased learning. We address these problems with three contributions: we (1) develop policy learning algorithms under runtime-confounding, (2) develop semi-parametric efficient off-policy estimation procedures, and (3) provide diagnostics for understanding the price of runtime confounding.

authors.name: Raphael Kim, Michele Santacatterina, Ramin Zabih, Keith Barnatchez

papers.title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
papers.summary: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on vision-language backbones, tying policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. While recent world-action models mostly scale the video backbone and its data, we argue that the choice of latent space is just as critical, and that the policy should be trained natively in that space. We introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; it predicts future features with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art average RoboTwin 2.0 success under both clean-only and full training, and state-of-the-art LIBERO-Plus success with corrected instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competitors; with full training, its success scales with model size up to 2.1B. Its S and B policies run two to five times faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming both on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, and La-JEPA outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to $\pi_{0.5}$. A design study shows that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction improves the policy even when skipped at inference. Tailoring the policy's design, including its latent space, to control can thus matter more than the knowledge transferred from a pretrained generative backbone, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.

authors.name: Mateo Cl\'emente, George Z. Xue, Amin Abyaneh, Liheng Ma, Rui Heng Yang, Tongtong Cao, Zhanguang Zhang, Yingxue Zhang

papers.title: The Approximation Ratio of $k$-means++ Is $2\ln k+O(1)$
papers.summary: Given a finite set of points in Euclidean space, $k$-means clustering seeks $k$ centers that minimize the sum of squared distances from each point to its nearest center. The $k$-means++ algorithm chooses its first center uniformly at random from the data points and each subsequent center with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest center already chosen. Let $R_k$ be the worst-case ratio between the expected cost of the $k$ seeds chosen by $k$-means++ and the optimal $k$-means cost. In their seminal paper introducing $k$-means++, Arthur and Vassilvitskii (SODA 2007) showed that $2\ln k\le R_k\le8(\ln k+2)$, and Makarychev, Reddy and Shan (NeurIPS 2020) improved the upper bound to $5(\ln k+2)$. We prove that $R_k=2\ln k+O(1)$; more precisely, $2H_{k-1}+2\le R_k\le 2H_{k-2}+5$ for $k\ge2$, where $H_j$ is the $j$th harmonic number, so the two bounds differ by less than $3$. We also determine $R_2=5$ and $R_3=185/32$, with a unified proof of both upper bounds, and give a second family of lower bounds that exceeds $2H_{k-1}+2$ for $2\le k\le18$. Previous analyses bound the expected cost of a cluster just after it is first sampled by a constant times its optimal cost, and then charge that cost for the rest of the run. We track how a cluster's cost evolves after its first hit. At each subsequent draw, the probability of sampling that cluster again is exactly its share of the current cost. We show that the cost reductions from these later hits suffice, in expectation, to bring the leading coefficient down to $2$.

authors.name: Aravind Reddy

papers.title: Finite speed Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Kac processes and their applications in generative modeling
papers.summary: We study the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Kac (OU-K) process, where instead of a Brownian motion, a finite-speed Kac process defines the driving process. The OU-K process can be analyzed through a rescaled, time-inhomogeneous Kac process, characterized by a switching rate from the Kac part, and a convergence rate from the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) part. The law of this inhomogeneous Kac process describes the solution of a wave equation, the Euler-Poisson-Darboux (EPD) equation. For Kac switching rates being multiples of the OU convergence rate, we can explicitly derive this EPD solution via the sum of (the derivative of) two Legendre polynomials, restricted between two Dirac points representing the wave fronts. Using the framework of piecewise-deterministic Markov processes (PDMP), we describe the conditional velocity fields of the OU-K process via our polynomial-law-formula. This allows us to apply the OU-K process in a generative flow model. Since the OU-K velocity fields prove to be bounded by the finite Kac speed, the usual time truncations of diffusion models become unnecessary. We demonstrate advantages over diffusion and flow matching models in terms of generation sharpness on singular data sets, while achieving competitive results on CIFAR-10 image generation.

authors.name: Richard Duong, Janis Auffenberg, Gabriele Steidl

papers.title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
papers.summary: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $\pi_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $\pi_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

authors.name: Jiaming Tang, Zhuoyang Zhang, Junxian Guo, Fangzhou Zhao, Yilong Zhao, Zekai Li, Xingyang Li, Yuyang Zhao, Song Bian, Zhijian Liu, Song Han

papers.title: Grounding Language Models in Speech Does Not Fix "AI Flavor": Calibrated LLM Judges, Goodhart Traps, and a Preference-Tuning Fix
papers.summary: Chinese outputs of large language models carry a perceptible "AI flavor": formulaic sentence frames, stacked written-register connectives, repetition loops, and layout leakage. A popular hypothesis blames text-only training for the missing inner-speech layer of human writing; injecting speech or prosody signals should therefore reduce it. We test it with controlled interventions on a 0.6B model; all three fail: (i) phoneme-interleaved continued pretraining yields no spokenness gain under text-matched controls while raising repetition (+0.13 [+0.03, +0.23]); (ii) prosody-plan conditional generation reaches an adherence of only 0.257 against a pre-registered 0.50 gate; (iii) a rule-based reward built on TTS prosody-feature distance is not distinguishable in double-blind evaluation by either humans (8/16) or a calibrated LLM judge (9/16). A root cause is evaluation: single-rater blind evaluation at n~20 only detects extreme (>=85%) preferences. We therefore build a calibrated LLM-judge protocol: the judge passes catch trials on known-answer pairs (16/16; pilots 22/24 and 24/24, versus 0.75 for the human rater), then annotates with two independent judges under A/B swap, disagreement counted as a tie. Using the judge's agree labels directly as DPO pairs (no reward model), we obtain the first positive result: held-out blind win rate 0.833 (tie=0.5; bootstrap CI [0.708, 0.938]; hard-agree 0.900 [0.699, 0.972]), repetition 0.114 to 0.000, MMLU within noise. We further identify a Goodhart channel: the judge's length preference transduces into output-length collapse via pairwise DPO (median 75 chars vs a 300-char prompt); an SFT-anchor repairs it (w is a style knob: w=0.1 preserves gains). Scaling preference data from 89 to 240 pairs yields no additional judge-visible gain. We release RA-Eval v0.1: a three-layer Chinese AI-flavor evaluation framework with 382 judge-annotated preference pairs.

authors.name: Dongwu Qian

papers.title: Represented but misread: Post-training changes how language models read out what they represent
papers.summary: Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models' own answers, analyzed with signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. For judgments of whether German texts were written by a human or an AI, probes and word n-gram classifiers separated the classes well, but the answers did not and often ordered the texts inversely. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average ($\Delta d' = -0.34$ across model families; -0.29 across three prompts). It also changed the use of a stated base rate: Base models shifted their log-odds by less than the stated change in prior odds, most post-trained models by more. In two models with stage-wise checkpoints, the change occurred during supervised fine-tuning, model stitching implicated the early layers, and from mid-depth on internal states at positions after the text, not those of the text, transferred the change between checkpoints. Our corpora cannot be shared, so we add a case reproducible from public data, the truth of negated statements. Here, post-training acted in the opposite direction: Probes decoded truth at or near ceiling in every model, the answers of several base models did not use it, and post-training repaired them; by mid-depth the repair resided at the positions after the statement; below it, the representation of the statement contributed, strongly in one of four models. In a training study, adding 2,000 correctly labeled authorship judgments of news texts to otherwise identical fine-tuning data improved the answers on our newspaper and textbook corpora and inverted them on the chats, where they followed a news-trained probe of the base model. Post-training thus changed how a judgment is read out of what a model represents, and a small training signal can set its direction.

authors.name: Jochen Laubrock

papers.title: SkillPrivus: Uncovering PRIVacy of USe Harms in Agentic Skills
papers.summary: Agent skills extend AI assistants through installable instructions and code that can access users' files, accounts, and data. Even when performing their advertised tasks, skills may infer sensitive attributes, retain unnecessary information, or disclose data to unexpected recipients. We study these potential privacy-of-use harms through SkillPrivus, a static audit framework that analyzes skills before installation without executing them. SkillPrivus extracts data operations from code and natural-language instructions, grounds them in source evidence, and adapts Contextual Integrity to assess their appropriateness. Applied to 726 real skills from public marketplaces, 563 of which handle personal data, SkillPrivus flags at least one potential violation in 307 of these skills (54.5%), and its judgments agree with three blind human annotators on 83.2% of resolvable moves. The flagged behaviors include sensitive inferences, information use beyond the stated task, and disclosures to unexpected recipients, suggesting that privacy harms can arise from ordinary skill functionality.

authors.name: Mariana Fernandez-Espinosa, Ivoline Ngong, Keerthiram Murugesan, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Unlearns Corrupted SFT Reasoning
papers.summary: We show that reinforcement learning (RL) in reasoning tasks can succeed even when the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data is severely corrupted. In a mathematical reasoning dataset (GSM8K), we systematically corrupt training trajectories across 361 configurations by injecting realistic error types, varying error locations, trace-answer consistency, and corruption ratios up to 100%. While aggregated SFT-only performance steadily deteriorates under corruption (dropping from 43.61% to 13.80%), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training consistently restores model accuracy back to gold-baseline levels (approximately 60%). Crucially, initializing RL with as few as N = 8 minimal, incorrect, three-line "form-only" traces boosts post-RL performance to 69.30%, outperforming standard gold SFT initialization (60.71%) and GRPO without SFT (35.00%). Further, we show that SFT accuracy is largely uncorrelated with post-RL accuracy (r approximately 0), demonstrating a fundamental asymmetry in post-training: SFT primarily establishes structural layout (form), while RL independently discovers functional reasoning (function).

authors.name: Anika Misra, Shreyas Vinod, Huteng Dai

papers.title: Know Your Context Bank: Repairing Inconsistency and Measuring Generalization in Context-Aware Text-to-SQL
papers.summary: Text-to-SQL systems increasingly rely on context banks: curated collections of example queries, metric definitions, and domain knowledge that tell a model how an organization writes its queries. In the enterprise, a bank grows over years as many analysts add entries, checked one at a time for correctness (does the SQL answer its own question?) and rarely for consistency with one another. Yet correctness is often loosely defined: a question seldom fixes how an entity is counted or which table defines it, so two entries can each pass review yet resolve the same decision in opposite ways. We call this condition context bank rot. A second question follows: does a system that uses a bank generalize from it, or only reproduce it? Existing benchmarks cannot tell, as they do not control how far a test question sits from the context. We answer both questions by comparing queries decision by decision, with a fast scorer distilled from human-calibrated LLM judges. Turned inward, the comparison diagnoses and repairs a bank. Fine-tuning on a cleaned BIRD-train bank beats a same-size random subset at every epoch (+2.6 points on average), and 92.4% of our removals had their SQL corrected by an independent expert audit, against 45.6% of audited entries. In-context examples that follow one convention beat those following the opposite one by 13.3 points, while a mix is barely better than none. Turned outward, the comparison generates test questions at a controlled distance from a bank, a pipeline we call CAT (Context-Aware Testing). On CAT-BIRD, for retrieval and fine-tuning alike, the benefit of a bank falls step by step with distance and is largely gone once about three quarters of a question's logic is new, and on CAT-Spider the benefit of retrieval likewise shrinks with distance.

authors.name: Hailong Li, Mohammadreza Pourreza, Tal Neiman, Reza Sherkat, Per Jacobsson, Yannis Papakonstantinou

papers.title: Cross-Linguistic Distinctive-Feature Constraints on Segmental Triphones: Evidence for Contrastive Dispersion
papers.summary: Natural speech reflects articulatory and perceptual constraints, yet how these pressures shape consecutive segment transitions across languages remains underexplored. We analyze adjacent distinctive-feature distances in token-weighted segmental triphones across 17 Universal Dependencies corpora spanning nine language families, transcribed into IPA and mapped to 24 PanPhon features using Hamming and cosine metrics. Natural sequences exhibit an intermediate-distance mode (8-10 features under Hamming, except Vietnamese; 0.28-0.38 under cosine). Against an unrestricted within-word shuffled baseline, natural words reject the inventory-only null (W = 0, p < 10-4), showing higher expected distance, narrower dispersion, and lower joint triphone entropy in all 17 languages. Under a stricter within-word consonant-vowel template baseline, expected distance and dispersion are no longer separated, whereas joint entropy remains lower in 16 languages (p = 1.07x10-4). Entropy decomposition reveals higher mutual information between incoming and outgoing transitions in all 17 languages and all nine families (W = 0, p < 10-4), demonstrating sequential coupling beyond syllable-template alternation. Word-level mean-SD correlations and directional asymmetries do not replicate cross-linguistically.

authors.name: Leonardo Ara\'ujo

papers.title: Weight-Space Programming Writes In-Context Learning and Matches Fine-Tuning in Language Models
papers.summary: Weight-space programming is a frontier language model's recently reported ability to read and rewrite another network's weights without gradient descent. We investigate how examples can provide a weight update so that a weaker language model performs the task with nothing in the prompt, and study what it edits. Our experiments cover six tasks, four frontier editors and three families of weaker language models, without the editors being told anything about in-context learning (ICL). In most runs, the few-shot minus zero-shot residual is measured at the final prompt token, the ICL task vector, and write it into the weights, at its sparsest into near-silent MLP units keyed to the prompt format. Results reach the accuracy of ICL and of fine-tuning on the same examples, LoRA included, usually leaving perplexity untouched, with worse performance under changes of wording. We also qualify the comparison by counting unfinished runs, observing that one editor falls below fine-tuning; held only to the seen examples, without task pairs of their own, only the strongest editor has similar performance. Given a task and unlabelled inputs, that editor writes its own examples and does nearly as well on unseen items as with labels.

authors.name: Konstantinos Skianis, Aristidis Likas

papers.title: How Long Will My Language Model Run? A Benchmark for Pre-Execution Runtime Prediction
papers.summary: Researchers submitting deep learning jobs to shared GPU clusters need runtime estimates to request time limits, choose hardware, and budget compute. Large language models (LLMs) offer a tempting shortcut: describe the job and ask. We introduce PreRun, a benchmark for predicting deep learning training and inference runtime from information available before execution. PreRun contains 801 training and 1,884 inference records of language and vision models collected on a GPU cluster, paired with workload configurations and explicitly defined timing targets. It also includes 64 text-generation configurations measured under standardized conditions, each in three separate program launches. We compare three LLMs (Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Claude Opus 5.5) with regression baselines and evaluate analytical estimates on a supported forward-pass subset. On 16 held-out generation configurations, the open-weight LLMs underestimate latency by 90-99% on average without examples. Claude's zero-shot mean absolute error is 4.5 times that of a Random Forest fit on 32 configurations. Five labeled examples substantially reduce Claude's generation error, but their benefit varies across timing targets. We will open-source our data and evaluation pipeline upon acceptance.

authors.name: Ashish Molakalapalli, Kangda Wei, Haonan Duan, Alex Carter, Ruihong Huang

papers.title: Isolating the Language Shell: A Content-Controlled Study of Multilingual Reasoning
papers.summary: Multilingual reasoning distillation requires choosing the language in which teacher reasoning is presented, yet existing recipes often entangle linguistic form with differences in generation, translation, and filtering. We construct content-controlled supervision by rendering the same verified English trajectories into English, translated target-language, and language-mixed shells, and fine-tune two pretrained students in three target languages, evaluating them on multilingual mathematical reasoning at two difficulty levels. Even with the underlying reasoning content held fixed, we find that shell choice can change downstream accuracy, with effects varying across students, languages, and difficulty levels. Pre-training compatibility does not consistently track these outcomes, and even when our tests find no clear accuracy difference between shells, their output-language behavior can still differ substantially. These results suggest that the supervision shell is a distinct design choice in multilingual reasoning distillation.

authors.name: Hoejoon Kwon, Jinhee Jang, Byeonggeuk Lim, YoungBin Kim

papers.title: NightmareDiscourseBench: A Benchmark Dataset for Fictional Direct Discourse Identification Pipelines
papers.summary: In this paper we introduce a new benchmark dataset, NightmareDiscourseBench, for testing NLP pipelines that identify forms of direct discourse in English-language fiction. We first review existing publicly available benchmarks (providing summary statistics and reviewing available metadata) for this task, identifying theoretical inconsistency and exclusive focus on speech as primary issues in this domain. We then overview our narrative theory-based framework for classifying and evaluating different forms of direct discourse, and finally describe NightmareDiscourseBench, a new benchmark test set of 12 text samples accompanied by metadata pertinent to the task of direct discourse identification.

authors.name: Claudia Carroll, Gabi Kirilloff, Dashiell Leigh

papers.title: When Do LLM-Elicited Priors Help? A Controlled Audit of Language Models as Priors for Small-Sample Bayesian Regression
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked where to center the coefficients of a small-sample Bayesian regression, but the evidence is unclear: benchmarks are often built to match the prior and models may remember them. We audit this practice with one frontier and one flash-tier model, using hidden feature names, post-cutoff housing data and a pre-specified test that gives features the wrong descriptions. First, the models share their errors (correlation $0.92$--$0.99$ across draws, vendors and paraphrases): averaging $20$ draws is no more accurate than one, and treating draws as independent creates overconfidence. Much of this error comes from reporting each feature's effect alone, not with the others held fixed. Second, against the best classical prior, the LLM center helps clearly on one of four benchmarks (RMSE $-5.8\%$), marginally on two, and hurts mean RMSE on the fourth. Third, the LLM's stated uncertainty is unreliable; letting the data set the prior scale cuts the harm of a wrong center four-fold against a unit-variance prior. A pre-specified external test returned the verdict \textsc{partial}: on $18$ rule-selected problems the center helps on six and hurts on four, and a hard trust gate trusts a harmful prior while an evidence-weighted mixture is safer.

authors.name: Ran Zou, Yang Liu

papers.title: How Far Does Lossless Re-tokenization Move an RLVR Update?
papers.summary: Language models assign different probabilities to token sequences that decode to the same string. In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), a trainer that re-encodes sampled text may train on a different token sequence with the same reward. We ask how far this moves a training update, and whether the movement has a consistent direction. From one checkpoint, we compare updates on the same rollouts, canonical and with selected tokens split into two pieces, against an update on a different batch. On Qwen2.5-0.5B with three-digit addition, splitting about one token in 25 moves the update 0.556 times as far as replacing the batch. The ratio rises with the fraction split in four models and depends on which tokens are split; within a checkpoint, the displacements share a direction across batches. In a tabular model with one table per tokenization and a single sampled string, we prove that whenever two strings below an unsampled prefix differ in probability, only the zero full-gradient step agrees across tokenizations, however it is weighted. In an audit that decodes and re-encodes resampled rollouts, re-encoding touches up to 5.2% of rollouts but at most 0.08% of tokens, far below the split fractions we test. Training on fixed rollouts, the canonical arm finishes ahead in 14 of 18 pre-registered pairs; the interval for the mean accuracy difference includes zero over all pairs and excludes it only under the registered exclusion rule, which favours the canonical arm.

authors.name: Zhe Dong, Fang Qin

papers.title: Cross-Platform Production Signatures of State-Linked Information Operations
papers.summary: An information operation active on several platforms presents different names, personas, and topics on each. Its working routine is harder to change. We call this routine the operation's production signature: the regularities in when and how its accounts post, reply, and repost. We measure it from timestamps and coarse action types only, using no content, profile metadata, or network ties, as timing and action profiles for accounts and learned action-gap policies for populations. We then ask which parts of a signature carry over to another platform and which belong to a single operation. We train models on Twitter archives of four state-linked operations and apply them to Internet Research Agency (IRA) accounts on Reddit, with no Reddit training labels. They rank the IRA accounts at AUC 0.90-0.94. Content detectors on the same route fall from 0.98 within a platform to 0.81. Daily phase accounts for most of the transfer. Posting volume reverses direction between platforms, and action mix follows the role accounts hold on each platform. What transfers is not unique to the IRA: a second operation shares the same working-hours window, and action-gap policies separate every operation from organic accounts (AUC 0.96-1.0) without consistently ranking their own operation first. On 938 Telegram channels, groups that forward the same sources keep ordinary hours and pace but publish original posts in the same ten-minute windows more often than chance. This pattern is invisible when accounts are examined one at a time. Our results suggest that timing and action traces learned on one platform can help flag likely operations on another.

authors.name: Lin Tian, Marian-Andrei Rizoiu

papers.title: How Much of a Calculation-Error Rate Is Not Arithmetic: Auditing the FinReason Cup 2026 Task 3 Metric with a Deterministic Rule System
papers.summary: Task 3 of the FinReason Cup 2026 scores a system on two values per case, the one an XBRL filing reports and the one its own calculation relationships imply, and labels each failure as structural, extraction or calculation. This report shows that the calculation-error rate so defined does not count arithmetic failures, and bounds how far it is from one using the published board alone. One of the three rules behind the benchmark, DQC_US_0015, has an answer that is the negation of the reported value (in all 110 published practice cases, against 1 of 120 and 6 of 102 for the other two), so a calculation label on such a case records a wrong fact or a wrong route, not a wrong sum. Subtracting the available structural and extraction labels from each entry's error count on that rule gives a floor: the bound is positive for 22 of the 23 ranked entries, and at the top it is sharpest, with at least 11 of 12 and 12 of 13 calculation errors of the two joint-first entries falling on cases where no arithmetic remained. The calculation-error rate of the best systems on this task is almost entirely not arithmetic. The vehicle for that result is an entry that reconstructs the three data-quality rules the benchmark is drawn from, DQC_US_0015, DQC_US_0117 and DQC_US_0126, as a deterministic system with no learned parameters, no training step and no external service, running all 680 cases in 1.4 seconds. It scores 96.62% under the offline judge on development and 95.29% on the published test set, and its residual error concentrates in cases where a concept carries several equally flagged facts and the question names no dimensional member. Reading those error classes against the per-rule accuracies is what exposed the metric, which is why both are reported here.

authors.name: Vladimir Beskorovainyi

papers.title: CoPyro: Feeding Copy Proposals to Parallel Drafters
papers.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates language generation by letting a target model verify several draft tokens in one forward pass. Earlier neural drafters such as EAGLE extend each candidate sequence one token at a time. Recent work has turned to parallel drafters such as DFlash, which predict a whole block at once. Another approach uses n-gram retrieval to find an earlier occurrence of the current context suffix and copy the tokens that followed it directly into the draft. We introduce CoPyro, which feeds these copied tokens into a parallel drafter in place of masks. The drafter learns from context which tokens to keep and which to revise as it predicts the block in its usual forward pass. Across eight benchmarks on Qwen3-4B, CoPyro improves overall acceptance length for all four parallel drafters tested, with gains of 2.19-5.08% when trained on 100K samples. With DFlash trained on 710K samples, overall gains range from 1.08% to 2.00% across the tested model sizes and temperatures. Code generation benefits most in both settings. On Qwen3-8B, processing the proposals adds an average of 0.24 ms per decoding round in Transformers.

authors.name: Hong-Kai Zheng, Piji Li

papers.title: LongCat Recall Sparse Attention: Co-Designing Key Organization and Retrieval for Long-Context Inference
papers.summary: Retrieval-based sparse attention, exemplified by DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), reduces attention computation by selecting a small subset of key-value entries. However, selecting these entries can still require searching the entire visible history. For long sequences, retrieval becomes a major bottleneck, limiting the efficiency gains from sparse attention. To address this problem, we propose LongCat Recall Sparse Attention (LRSA), which combines fine-grained representatives with paged retrieval in an incrementally maintained index. LRSA partitions the sequence into time buckets that can be indexed independently as new keys arrive, without regrouping existing history. Within each bucket, it organizes indexing keys into capacity-balanced directional groups and packs a fixed number of complete groups into each page, retaining a separate center for every group. These centers provide fine-grained representatives for page selection, after which refinement scores members of the selected pages together with sink, sliding-window, and visible unindexed candidates to select the final Top-$K$ logical positions. To execute this retrieval process efficiently, we store members in reordered pages, fuse construction stages according to group size, and share storage for overlapping fixed candidates across queries during chunked prefill. These choices support regular member access while reducing kernel launches during construction and repeated candidate transfers. Moreover, we integrate LRSA into SGLang to maintain the index during inference, overlapping asynchronous index construction for new buckets with subsequent computation and reusing compatible bucket indices and member pages after a prefix match in the original key-value pool. With a 1024K-token context, LRSA accelerates key selection by 4.70$\times$ over DSA and combined selection and attention by 35.60$\times$ over full attention.

authors.name: Hao Zhang, Bin Xiao, Kefeng Zhang

papers.title: Do Companies Deliver on Their IPO Claims?
papers.summary: Initial public offering (IPO) filings describe what a company does and what it intends to become. Yet whether individual forward-looking claims are subsequently realized is difficult to assess. We introduce Vision Follow-Through (VFT), a benchmark and agentic pipeline that separates claim extraction, category assignment, verifiability, and evidence-grounded follow-through assessment. \vftclaims{} contains 5,066 human-annotated claim spans from 50 IPO filings, while \vftverify{} adds verifiability tiers, follow-through outcomes, and cited later evidence for 1,000 claims. Across language models, classifying human-annotated claims is substantially easier than extracting claims from full filings. Extraction coverage also varies sharply by category, with Organizational/Culture claims recovered far less often than Market Opportunity claims. Follow-through assessment poses a separate challenge: model judgments diverge from human assessments in different ways rather than exhibiting a single consistent bias. These results show that reliable assessment of corporate follow-through requires both finding the relevant claims and grounding subsequent judgments in later evidence.

authors.name: Vidhyakshaya Kannan, Shiv Banafar, Michael Galarnyk, Sagnik Nandi, Soumeya Kannan, Shauray Arora, Abanoub Abdelmalak, Sudheer Chava

papers.title: Observed, Curated, Reused: Observation Bias in Clinical AI Evaluation
papers.summary: Clinical AI evaluations are vulnerable to observation bias embedded in routine medical documentation, which captures only what clinicians notice, test, and record rather than a complete clinical picture. As this evidence travels into publications and reference knowledge graphs, crucial distinctions disappear: unexamined symptoms blur with confirmed negatives, and chronological disease progression is lost. Surviving evidence can also enter both the benchmark query and the reference knowledge base, creating a self-referential loop where a patient is evaluated against clues derived from their own published case report. To quantify this bias, we tracked 6,503 clinical cases across six historical Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) releases (October 2021-June 2026) to identify when HPO first cited the publications describing them. This yielded a confirmatory cohort with an observable "source ingestion" event, where HPO cited a case's source publication as target-disease evidence. Diagnostic rankers depended heavily on these source publications: for our primary semantic ranker (Resnik), publication-weighted mean reciprocal rank rose from 0.26 before paper ingestion to 0.84 upon inclusion in HPO, but collapsed to 0.05 when source-linked assertions were counterfactually removed. Two additional rankers (IC-cosine and LIRICAL) reproduced this trajectory, and control experiments confirmed the diagnostic jump was driven by the patient's publication rather than background HPO growth. Clinical AI systems may therefore score well because their knowledge base contains evidence linked to the test case's source publication, rather than through generalization. Modern knowledge is not the problem; evaluation evidence must match the claim. Trustworthy benchmarks must separate patients, source-linked evidence, and time: historical tests should use only knowledge available at the intended decision time.

authors.name: Md Shamim Ahmed, Lukas Galke Poech, Richard R\"ottger

papers.title: Breaking the Long Horizon: Short-Horizon Process Supervision for Long-Form Generation in LLMs
papers.summary: Long-form generation is increasingly important for agentic LLM systems, yet current reinforcement learning methods typically optimize an entire document with a single outcome-level reward. This delayed and coarse-grained supervision makes it difficult to localize errors and assign credit across semantically distinct parts of the output. To address this, we propose a short-horizon framework that reformulates long-form generation through semantic decomposition into segment-level decisions. Each segment is generated with prefix-conditioned context, allowing cross-segment coherence to be preserved while keeping supervision local. The generated segments are then scored with rubric-based rewards for adherence, coherence, and relevance, enabling explicit local supervision at the segment level. These local rewards are used to compute step-wise advantages, yielding localized policy updates. To isolate the effect of supervision granularity, we instantiate both outcome-level supervision and our short-horizon process reward method (SH-PRM) under the same GRPO framework. Across multiple LLMs and two long-form generation benchmarks, SH-PRM consistently outperforms outcome-level supervision and strong inference-time baselines under the same optimizer and comparable budgets. Further analyses suggest that these gains primarily arise from improved credit assignment. Overall, our results suggest that aligning supervision granularity with the semantic structure of long-form generation is an effective design principle for long-form LLM training.

authors.name: Heyang Xu, HanWen Hao, Qianren Mao, Zhuo Liu, Qili Zhang, Sheng Yang, Jianxin Li

papers.title: Silent Arbitration: How Large Language Models Resolve Co-Authoritative Conflicting Instructions
papers.summary: Large language models increasingly receive high-level instructions about roles, values, interests, and communication style. Such instructions can conflict even when a prompt assigns them equal authority and provides no priority rule. We study co-authoritative persona conflict, in which a single prompt jointly assigns two opposing personas. Across eight conflict types grounded in published source material and five LLMs, we measure conflict acknowledgment, resolution strategy, and directional stance. Models acknowledge incompatibility in 72% of direct checks but explicitly surface it in only 22% of task responses, revealing silent arbitration. Dominance accounts for 45% of dual-persona responses, and 35% of compromise-labeled responses retain directional lean. Prompt framing further changes the visible form of arbitration substantially more than ordinary paraphrase variation. These findings show that evaluating instruction following should assess whether models disclose conflicts, how they resolve them, and which persona their responses favor.

authors.name: Sihyeon Lee, Jiwoo Kum, Jihun Song, Chanwoo Kim, Chanjun Park

papers.title: Structurally Different, Functionally Persistent: Capability Regions Under Model Optimization
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) capabilities have been associated with localized parameter regions, enabling targeted model editing and intervention. However, it remains unclear whether a region identified before model optimization remains an effective intervention target afterward. We evaluate the functional persistence and parameter overlap of coding capability regions across three instruction-tuned models under quantization, pruning, and LoRA-based adaptation. Although re-extracted regions exhibit substantial parameter reorganization, ablating the original region after optimization eliminates or nearly eliminates coding performance in almost all conditions, while magnitude-matched controls preserve performance. Partition analysis further shows that the shared subset of the original and re-extracted regions accounts for most of the observed ablation effect in the majority of conditions. These results demonstrate that parameter overlap and functional persistence are distinct: capability regions can remain causally effective intervention targets even when their parameter realization changes substantially.

authors.name: Jiwoo Kum, Chanwoo Kim, Doyun Kim, Seonghyeon Cho, Sihyeon Lee, Chanjun Park

papers.title: Typhoon OCR 2: From Thai Document Transcription to Multilingual, Multi-Task OCR
papers.summary: Typhoon OCR 1.5 focused on reading Thai documents. However, in real-world workflows, users often need to extract specific information or preserve the structure of an entire page for further processing. Typhoon OCR 2 handles both tasks in a single model, with prompt-driven extraction and structured full-page parsing. Full-page parsing covers Thai, English, and Chinese. We release compact 2B and 0.8B models adapted from open document parsers through supervised fine-tuning on curated Thai and public multilingual data, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task rewards and a rule penalizing unfinished responses. Among evaluated open models, Typhoon OCR 2 2B scores highest on Thai MDPBench (80.7 versus 68.9 for Typhoon OCR 1.5) and on ThaiOCRBench (59.91 versus 40.45), which covers recognition, extraction, and document understanding. The 2B model remains close to its base on English olmOCR-bench (84.7 versus 84.4) and on OmniDocBench, which evaluates English and Chinese together (90.97 versus 91.03). On MDPBench, GRPO reduces the mean share of pages with repetition loops for the 2B model from 3.2% to 0.7%, with a smaller and statistically uncertain score gain for the 0.8B model. We release the model weights, Python package, and evaluation suite.

authors.name: Surapon Nonesung, Natapong Nitarach, Sittipong Sripaisarnmongkol, Kunat Pipatanakul, Warit Sirichotedumrong

papers.title: How Many Bytes Has a BPE Model Seen? Estimating Byte-Token Exposure in Pretraining from Corpus Statistics and Embedding Norms
papers.summary: Byte-level BPE vocabularies retain 256 single-byte fallback tokens. When converting such a model into a pure byte-level model, these tokens provide the starting embeddings. How much training have they received? We estimate byte-token exposure in Qwen3.8 using two independent routes. First, we tokenize 540 MB of public corpora covering 40 domains and 33 languages, then combine per-domain token shares with assumed pretraining mixtures. Single-byte tokens account for 13 to 36% of tokens, mostly ASCII; genuine UTF-8 fallback bytes (0x80-0xFF) account for 0.15 to 0.27% under mainstream mixtures, or about 2 billion occurrences per trillion pretraining tokens. Fallback rates vary by four orders of magnitude across languages, reflecting how well each script is covered by the vocabulary. Second, we analyze embedding and output-matrix row norms for four open models, using untrained padding rows as a zero-exposure baseline and ordinary tokens with known frequencies for calibration. In all four models, the 13 bytes that cannot occur in valid UTF-8 remain at initialization, while every legal high byte lies in a high-frequency band. For Qwen3.8, the norm-based estimate agrees with the corpus estimate within a factor of four. The norm-frequency relation eventually folds, so inversion is useful only as a model-specific, order-of-magnitude estimate. No private data were used.

authors.name: Liwei Zhang, ZhiMing Tong, Mochen Guan, Linzhe Li

papers.title: Open CDLM: A Benchmark and Library for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.summary: Reliable comparisons of continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) require evaluating both model fit and the distribution of generated text. Two common practices leave this goal only partially addressed. Likelihood-based evaluation often reports a variational upper bound on discrete negative log-likelihood, whose slack can confound comparisons. Generated-sample-based evaluation commonly combines generative perplexity with within-sequence unigram entropy; both scores can remain favorable even when a sampler produces the same text on every draw. We introduce \textbf{Open CDLM}, a benchmark for evaluating CDLMs and their samplers, and describe the design of an accompanying open-source library to support reproducible comparisons. For likelihood-based evaluation, we clarify which comparisons of model fit are supported by reported perplexity bounds and how those conclusions depend on the evaluation procedure. For sample-based evaluation, we use \textit{Kernel Text Discrepancy} (\textbf{KTD}) to compare collections of generated and real texts, alongside diagnostics for diversity, validity, and coverage. In controlled OpenWebText experiments, replacing a collection of texts with copies of a single selected passage improves both conventional generation scores. MAUVE detects the resulting collapse, and its response to other perturbations depends on the text representation and the type of perturbation. This work marks the beginning of Open CDLM as an open-source project for CDLM research. We will maintain and extend the library over time and welcome contributions from the community.

authors.name: Hao Jiang, Ruixi Chen, Jiayi Han, Yulei Sun, Yujian Chen, Gen Li, Brian. K Chen, Guang Cheng, Weijian Luo, Tianyang Hu

papers.title: Alliance Rupture and Repair in Simulating Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Dialogues
papers.summary: In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), routine work can strain the client-counselor working alliance, and the counselor must then notice the rupture, repair it, and adapt the work that follows. Existing CBT simulators model client resistance and follow structured treatment plans, but rarely track alliance state or allow counselors to repair ruptures over multiple turns and revise their plans accordingly. We present ALLY, a simulation framework that brings alliance rupture, repair, and replanning into ongoing CBT dialogue. Each client has a hidden alliance state that governs how openly the client engages. Like a real counselor, the counselor agent sees only the dialogue. It must notice when the client pulls back or pushes against the work, repair the rupture, and replan the rest of the session around what it has learned. Automatic evaluation shows that ALLY's counselors are closer to real CBT counselors than those of existing public synthetic datasets in strategy flow and emotional dynamics, and that ALLY is rated highest overall in counseling quality (CTRS) and interpersonal skill (FIS-T). An expert evaluation with 20 licensed therapists also finds the simulated ruptures plausible and the repairs and replanning largely appropriate.

authors.name: Jian Chai, Yitian Yang, Siqi Liu, Yi-Chia Wang, Yi-Chieh Lee

papers.title: Auditing Post-Training Unlearning in Diffusion Language Models using Sparse Autoencoders
papers.summary: Machine unlearning is an approach to privacy protection: it aims to remove the influence of designated data while preserving the model's behavior on information that should be retained.
